name: Miami-Illinois

catalog_locator: Costa 2003 pp. 107, 108, 109, 110, 112, 113, 114 (page numbers as returned by Google Books view); Costa 1991 p. 40
catalog_quote: [Costa 2003:107] In Miami - Illinois, there is a rule placing accent that operates separately from the strong syllable rule . [108] the accent rule counts syllables starting at the end of the word proceeding leftward, whereas the strong syllable rule starts at the beginning of words and proceeds rightward ... 3.2.8 . Final accent Bisyllabic words with short first vowels followed by preaspirates regularly take accent on their final syllables in Miami - Illinois . [109] 3.2.9 . Penultimate accent However, it is much more common for Miami - Illinois words to be accented on their penultimate syllables . This is the case in all bisyllabic words without a word - medial preaspirate ... [110] Similarly, in most words of more than two syllables, penultimate accent is basic ... [112] Apparently the rule accenting penultimate syllables in fact places accent on every other syllable starting from the end of the word ... [113] if a weak syllable is subject to devoicing, it cannot receive accent . [114] Accent retraction Words with long vowels in their preantepenultimate syllables regularly take accent on the antepenultimate syllable . I call this rule accent retraction, as it can be viewed as pulling the accent one syllable back from the expected penultimate position . [Costa 1991:40] Miami-Illinois has a rule of even-numbered syllable stress resembling that of Ojibwa, and a rule stressing penultimate syllables as well.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Miami (miam1252) is not in the catalog. The sole works with stress in the title, Carter, López Valdez & Sims 2020 (American Speech 95(2):119-148, doi 10.1215/00031283-7726313), is about Miami, Florida English (Spanish-contact rhythm/nPVI and vowels) and is mis-filed by Glottolog under the Algonquian language; abstract confirmed via Crossref and Semantic Scholar, full text paywalled (not reachable by automated download) — irrelevant, priority none. The best first-hand stress statements for Miami-Illinois are David Costa's: the 2003 grammar (accent chapter pp. 107-118: penultimate accent basic, alternating right-to-left, independent of the iambic strong-syllable rule, with final-accent, devoiced-vowel and accent-retraction exceptions; not phonemic) is available only as Google Books snippets (already held by the project from the 9/16 search, one page hit re-verified); the open-access Costa 1991 PAC22 paper (p. 40, fully read held by the project) states in one sentence 'a rule of even-numbered syllable stress resembling that of Ojibwa, and a rule stressing penultimate syllables as well.' Costa 2008 PAC39 (p. 150) adds accent-retraction detail. Still unobtained: Costa 2003 full text (high priority; Harvard print / HathiTrust search-only), Costa 1994 Berkeley dissertation, Rhodes 1989 'Miami Vowel Reduction' (unpublished). New records saved and logged in

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is assigned right-to-left, independently of the left-to-right iambic 'strong syllable rule': the penultimate syllable is accented by default (all disyllables without medial preaspirate; most longer words). Two systematic departures: (a) a weak vowel devoiced before a preaspirate cannot carry accent, so disyllables like ahkí 'field', mahkwá 'bear' are final-accented and devoiced penults are skipped; (b) 'accent retraction': if the preantepenult has a long vowel, accent falls on the antepenult instead of the penult (eehsípana 'raccoon'), unless that antepenult is devoiced. Costa notes accent is not phonemic (2003:196 n.11).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Costa 2003:112: the penultimate rule 'places accent on every other syllable starting from the end of the word', so words of five or more syllables show accent on both the preantepenultimate and the penultimate (e.g. illíniiwíta, waapíkináahkwa per the Wikipedia rendering); no explicit primary/secondary ranking is visible in the snippets.
new_statements.exceptions: Final accent in disyllables with short V1 + preaspirate (3.2.8); voiceless (devoiced) vowels never accented (3.2.11); accent retraction to antepenult after a long preantepenultimate vowel, blocked if the antepenult is devoiced or if the penult precedes a preaspirate (3.2.12, pp. 114-118); special final accent on imperatives/hortatives (pp. 323-26, 387); accent retraction interacts with person marking in dependent verbs (p. 286-7; Costa 2008:150); second-syllable lengthening (3.2.13) can shift antepenultimate vs penultimate accent (p. 120).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent in citation forms as reconstituted philologically from 19th-20th c. transcriptions (Gatschet, Dunn, Michelson, Hockett acute marks); the language had no L1 speakers after the mid-20th c. and is now revitalized (Myaamia), so the description is documentary rather than instrumental. Costa distinguishes 'accent' (prominence) from metrical 'strong/weak' syllable status, which governs deletion/devoicing.
new_statements.identity_note: Costa 2003 and 1991 describe 'Miami-Illinois' as a single language covering the Miami, Wea, Peoria and Illinois (Kaskaskia etc.) dialects, reconstituted from 17th-20th c. written records; Glottolog miam1252 (ISO mia) is exactly this unit. The accent evidence comes mainly from late-19th/early-20th c. Miami and Peoria speakers recorded by Gatschet, Dunn and Michelson; Costa reports no dialect difference in accent in the material seen. Modern revitalized Myaamia follows Costa's analysis.

new_statements.citation: Costa, David J. 2003. The Miami-Illinois Language. Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press, ch. 3 sections 3.2.7-3.2.10, pp. 107-112 (Google Books snippet text; page numbers as returned by Google Books; p.110 hit independently re-verified 2026-09-17).
new_statements.reading: Word accent in Miami-Illinois is basically penultimate, assigned right-to-left in an alternating (trochaic-from-the-end) pattern; it is independent of the left-to-right iambic 'strong syllable rule' (which governs devoicing/lengthening). Systematic exceptions: final accent in bisyllables of the shape short V + preaspirate (and in imperatives); devoiced weak vowels cannot be accented and are skipped; 'accent retraction' onto the antepenult when the preantepenult vowel is long. Costa adds (p.196 n.11) that accent is not phonemic. Caveat: read only as Google Books snippet text, not the full page; the fully-read open-access Costa 1991 (PAC22, p.40) gives the same two-rule picture in one sentence.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Miami-Illinois language', section 'Suprasegmental processes > Accent' (citing Costa 2003: 114).
sources.quote: Otherwise, the accent is placed on every other syllable starting from the end of the word, beginning with the penultimate: illíniiwíta 'he is a man', waapíkináahkwa 'whooping crane'. Because of rule (1), the accent cannot land on voiceless vowels, and appears simply to ignore them for metrical purposes.
sources.note: Second-hand summary of Costa 2003: accent independent of strong-syllable rule, assigned right-to-left; (1) voiceless vowels never accented so ahkí, mahkwá final; (2) long vowel in preantepenult -> accent retraction; (3) otherwise every other syllable from the end starting with the penult (illíniiwíta, waapíkináahkwa).

sources.quote: It is beyond the scope of this paper to give a full discussion of the stress rules of Miami-Illinois (see Rhodes 1989 for a partial description), but suffice it to say that Miami-Illinois has a rule of even-numbered syllable stress resembling that of Ojibwa, and a rule stressing penultimate syllables as well.
sources.note: p. 40: 'It is beyond the scope of this paper to give a full discussion of the stress rules of Miami-Illinois (see Rhodes 1989 for a partial description), but suffice it to say that Miami-Illinois has a rule of even-numbered syllable stress resembling that of Ojibwa, and a rule stressing penultimate syllables as well.' Also notes Hockett and Michelson often transcribed short stressed vowels as long.
